newsitem.title: BELGIUM: UCB to continue profit plough-back policy.
newsitem.headline: UCB to continue profit plough-back policy.

text.p: Belgian chemicals, drugs and films group UCB said on Wednesday it would continue its policy of retaining a large part of profits in the company to fund its strategy of innovation and globalisation.
Asked about the likely 1996 dividend, chief executive officer Georges Jacobs told reporters, "We will continue to put a large part of profit back into the company."
"The pay-out ratio has been 30 to 35 percent...I am not saying (it will stay that way), I am saying so far we have done that," he said. UCB paid a 1995 dividend of 600 francs a share.

Analysts have forecast 1996 dividend of 700 to 750 francs and 800 to 825 in 1997. Generale Bank's Sandra Vandersmissen expected the 1996 dividend to be 750 francs on the assumption UCB would maintain its pay-out ratio.
Jacobs said he was "very confident that the innovation and globalisation process was well on track."

UCB's 1997 investment programme will total about 10 billion francs, he said. This would be funded internally. He noted the company's plough-back strategy had also helped UCB cut financial charges by half in 1996. This was a reflection of the group's strength and illustrative of its financial independence.

Jacobs reiterated that UCB was not volume-oriented, but looking for high value-added niches. "Our (small) size is a plus, I know what is happening in my research centre, when you are too big, you can't control it."

As an example of movement into a profitable niche, he cited the film sector and specifically the swing away from films for food, which dominated production four years ago, to films for non-food, which now take up 75 percent of output.
Recently, UCB concluded a deal with the Reserve Bank of Australia on the use of film in bank notes, where film added durability and copy protection.
The use of film includes putting a see-through plastic window in a banknote. "You can't photocopy such a note, you would get a black spot if you tried," Jacobs said.
UCB had recently closed a deal with Thailand on the use of films in banknotes, but business would not be fast growing. "People are attached to their notes...it is a political decision," Jacobs said.
Commenting on value added, he said, "Using the same material to wrap cheese and (in) a banknote, you can imagine the margin is a bit different."
